theme: Paul’s farewell to the Ephesian elders
readingInstruction: Read Acts 20:1-38. Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, raises Eutychus in Troas, and gives a farewell speech to the Ephesian elders at Miletus. Read the farewell slowly. It is Paul’s pastoral testament.
settingTheScene: Paul’s third missionary journey is drawing to a close. He is headed for Jerusalem with a collection for the poor saints there, knowing that chains and afflictions await. On the way he meets the elders of the Ephesian church on a beach at Miletus. This is the only speech in Acts that Paul gives to believers rather than to unbelievers, and it reveals his heart for the church.
observation: “On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them” (20:7).
“Testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ” (20:21).

“But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God” (20:24).
“For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (20:27).
“Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (20:28).
“And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified” (20:32).
“It is more blessed to give than to receive” (20:35).
“And there was much weeping on the part of all” (20:37).
interpretation:
At Troas, the church gathers on the first day of the week to break bread. Paul talks until midnight, and a young man, Eutychus, sitting in a window, falls asleep and falls three stories. He is taken up dead, and Paul embraces him and says, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” They go back upstairs, break bread, and talk until dawn. This verse is one of the clues that early Christians met on Sunday, the day of resurrection.

At Miletus, Paul summons the Ephesian elders and reminds them of how he lived among them. He served the Lord with all humility and with tears and trials. He did not shrink from declaring anything that was profitable, teaching in public and from house to house, testifying to both Jews and Greeks of repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus. Now, he says, he is going to Jerusalem, bound in the Spirit, not knowing what will happen, except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await him. “But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.” He says they will not see his face again.

Then comes his charge: “Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood.” The verse is rich: the Holy Spirit appoints pastors, the church belongs to God, and God bought it with his own blood, which is a striking reference to the cross. Paul warns that fierce wolves will come in, and even from among their own number men will arise speaking twisted things to draw away disciples. They must be alert. Within a few decades, the church of Ephesus had indeed faced such threats.

He commends them to God and to the word of his grace, “which is able to build you up.” The sufficiency of God’s word is the foundation of pastoral ministry. He reminds them of his example of working with his hands and quotes a saying of Jesus not found in the Gospels: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” Then he kneels and prays with them, and they all weep and kiss him, sorrowing most of all because they will not see his face again.
connection: Ezekiel 34 is a charge to shepherds. 1 Peter 5:1-4 is Peter’s charge to elders. 1 Timothy 3:1-7 and Titus 1:5-9 give qualifications for overseers. 2 Timothy 4:1-8 is Paul’s last charge to Timothy. Philippians 3:12-14 speaks of pressing on to finish the race. Ephesians 5:25 says Christ loved the church and gave himself for her. Hebrews 13:17 asks the church to submit to leaders who keep watch over souls. Revelation 2:1-7 is Christ’s later word to Ephesus.
application:
Ask how you can finish your course with joy. What is the ministry the Lord has given you?

Pray for your pastors and elders by name this week. Thank them.

Give something away, a gift of time or money, and experience the blessing Jesus spoke of.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the church he bought with his own blood.
Ask him to teach you to declare his whole counsel.
Ask him to help you care for those he has put in your life.
